title: 120 V 60 W incandescent lamp in a keyless holder on a base

sources.citation: The 120 V 60 W general-service incandescent lamp with a medium screw base, the common household lamp of NEC-region lighting circuits (lamp makers' catalogues, typical published ratings, paraphrased, not one vendor's). Its hot resistance is V² / P = 14400 / 60 = 240 Ω and its rated current P / V = 0.5 A.

L. L. Holladay, "Proportion of energy radiated by incandescent solids in various spectral regions", J. Opt. Soc. Am. 17 (1928), pp. 329–342, Table 5 (read 2026-11-12), paraphrased: regular gas-filled tungsten lamps of 50 W and 75 W run their filaments at a maximum of about 2685 K and 2735 K; a 60 W lamp interpolates to about 2705 K, and 2700 K is taken (the rounding is game-design). With tungsten's resistivity (Jones and Langmuir, 1927) it gives a cold resistance of 240 × 5.4849 / 81.095 = 16.23 Ω at 20 °C, 1/14.79 of the hot one, where the cold-start inrush comes from.

Physics from H. A. Jones and I. Langmuir, General Electric Review 30 (1927): a filament's cold-to-hot resistance ratio is ρ(T_r)/ρ(T_a), 13.5 to 16.1 for rated temperatures of 2500 to 2900 K at a 293 K ambient; 14.79 at this lamp's 2700 K. Source impedance and the wiring in series lower the current ratio, so the tested inrush band is 10 to 15 times the settled current.

Physics estimate (P3 decision D17, the τ ≈ 30 ms the realism review recommended in P2), recomputed in lamp-120v.spec.ts: a straight tungsten wire that radiates 95 % of 60 W at 2700 K with a total emissivity of about 0.317 (Holladay 1928, Table 3: 0.311 at 2600 K, 0.323 at 2800 K) and has 240 Ω there (ρ = 81.095 µΩ·cm, Jones and Langmuir) is about 43 µm × 440 mm, 12.5 mg at 19.3 g/cm³; with tungsten's heat capacity at 2700 K (36.19 J/(mol·K), NIST-JANAF table for crystalline tungsten, read 2026-11-12; 0.197 J/(g·K)) that is 2.46 mJ/K against a loss slope of 0.0857 W/K, τ ≈ 29 ms. A coiled filament's self-shading lengthens the wire and raises it (about 33 ms if 90 % of its surface radiates freely). 30 ms is taken; the model's heat capacity is then 2.57 mJ/K.

game-design inside published behaviour (P3 decision D17, paired with the 30 ms time constant as the realism review recommended in P2): 5 % of the rated power is lost by conduction at the rated point, the rest radiated. The model's light fits the published L ∝ V^3.4 (Fink and Beaty) best near 5 %. A long 120 V filament's end loss into its lead-ins is smaller than the bench lamp's (Langmuir, MacLane and Blodgett, Phys. Rev. 35, 1930: end losses are largest for short, thick, low-voltage filaments), and a gas-filled lamp also loses heat to its gas, which the vacuum model doesn't carry; the one linear term stands in for both. With it a switched-off filament's tail time constant is C / G = 2.57 mJ/K / 1.246 mW/K ≈ 2.1 s.

game-design: the lamp stands in a keyless porcelain holder on a 110 × 110 mm base, 150 mm tall with the lamp, with the brass (line) screw on one side and the silver (neutral) screw on the other; a stand-in for P4's lampholders and boxes (D12), not modelled on a product.

Makers' product pages for medium-base keyless incandescent lampholders with terminal screws give a terminal-screw torque range of 14 to 18 lb·in (1.6 to 2.0 N·m) (read 2026-11-12, paraphrased, not one vendor's). The fictional holder is marked 1.8 N·m (about 16 lb·in), inside it; NFPA 70-2023 Art. 110.14(D) requires the marked value (cited by number). No UL 486A-B torque table is used.

game-design: the holder's side-wired binding-head screws take one copper conductor each, 14 or 12 AWG, solid or stranded, wrapped clockwise under the head; not marked for aluminium. Stranded copper under a binding head splays (ADR 0018 §4.3). The 16 ± 3 mm strip wraps about three-quarters of a turn round the screw, and the head grips 12 mm of it. Usual for wiring-device side terminals, not published figures read for this entry.
game-design: conductors reach each screw from the base's side face and leave along ±x; not modelled on a product.
game-design: a slotted and Phillips combination head, common on wiring-device terminal screws (common practice, not one product); the drive type is a name and its size is not modelled.

NBS Building Science Series 103 (W. J. Meese and R. W. Beausoliel, 1977; read in the P3 source pre-audit, ADR 0018 §4.1): good branch-circuit wiring-device screw-terminal connections dropped 3 to 8 mV at 15 A, 0.2 to 0.5 mΩ. The class value 0.3 mΩ is taken as R₀, the contact resistance at the marked torque with a copper conductor at 20 °C; the engine scales it for torque, strip length, conductor count, strand spread and nicks (ADR 0018 §4).

game-design calibration (ADR 0018 §3.3, §11), the screw-terminal class's values: the heat path into the device, 0.026 W/K, is calibrated, not measured (with 14 AWG copper at 15 A it puts BSS 103's 18 to 36 W glowing connections between the Draper point, about 525 °C, and about 1000 °C); a porcelain holder conducts less than a breaker's body, which the class value doesn't distinguish. The clamp's heat capacity, 1.1 J/K, is a physics estimate: about 3 g of brass screw and terminal plate × about 380 J/(kg·K).
